facts.statement: The snipe-rail lived during the Late Holocene period.
The snipe-rail became extinct in the 13th century.
The genus Capellirallus was described by Falla in 1954.
The species name comes from Karamu Cave, located 21 km from Hamilton, where the holotype was found in 1954.
facts.quote: The species' name is derived from the Karamu Cave 21 km from Hamilton where the holotype was discovered in 1954.

facts.statement: The snipe-rail was an extinct flightless rail found only in the North Island of New Zealand.
facts.quote: The snipe-rail (Capellirallus karamu) is an extinct flightless rail endemic to the North Island of New Zealand.

facts.statement: The snipe-rail had a bill measuring about 7 cm, which was very long relative to its body size.
facts.quote: The snipe-rail was a relatively small rail which had a bill of about 7 cm, very long in proportion to its body size.

facts.statement: Relative to its body size, the snipe-rail possessed the smallest wings of any known rail species.
facts.quote: Relative to its body size, the snipe-rail had the smallest wings of all known rail species.

facts.statement: The snipe-rail had a disproportionately large tarsometatarsus.
facts.quote: It also had a disproportionately large tarsometatarsus.

facts.statement: Fossils of the snipe-rail were found in the western North Island, an area dominated by wet, closed-canopy rainforests.
facts.quote: The bone findings were in the western areas of the North Island, where wetter, closed-canopy rainforests prevailed.

facts.statement: Its long bill suggests the snipe-rail foraged by probing, similar to kiwi.
facts.quote: The bird's long bill suggests that it was able to forage by probing in a similar manner to kiwi.

facts.statement: It is debated when the snipe-rail went extinct, though researchers suggest its decline began in the 13th century due to the spread of the Polynesian rat.
facts.quote: The exact date of the snipe-rail's extinction is unknown, but it is supposed that the decline began in the 13th century, when the Kiori/Polynesian rat became widespread in New Zealand.

facts.statement: The evolutionary relationships of the snipe-rail are unclear, but its bone structure suggests it may be related to the extinct Chatham rail.
facts.quote: Its evolutionary relationships to other rail species are unclear but the structure of its bones suggests that it might have been a relative of the likewise extinct Chatham rail.

facts.statement: The snipe-rail belongs to the family Rallidae.
